been carried by the Liberals in the federal elections, notwithstanding the fact that Mr. McDonald was giving up his seat to his leader in order that he might take his place in the House of Commons, the Conservative opposition of the day and its supporters were not _ prepared to see that an election was avoided. In that particular contest a Conservative candidate was put in the field to oppose me. I was opposed, but the decency, the good sense and the chivalry of the electors of Prince Albert was shown by the fact that they gave me a majority of 5,621. That is how that majority came to be the size it was. I was supported in the constituency by men and women of all parties. May I contrast the attitude mentioned with what took place when Sir Robert Borden, at the time leader of the opposition, was defeated m a constituency in which he ran. Sir Robert Borden was chosen leader of his party, I think it. was m 1901. Could my right hon. friend give me the exact information?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My memory is that it
was around about 1901.

Sir Robert
was defeated in Halifax in 1904. It is interesting to observe that practically all the leaders of political parties in Canada-my right hon. friend says that he was defeated,
I thmk twice, but he was not then the leader -have been defeated at one time or another. This is almost inevitable, unless fortunately they are in very safe seats, due to the fact that they have had to give their time to the country as a whole rather than to their personal interests in their own constituencies. That is what happened to Sir Robert Borden in 1904. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Kidd) offered Sir Robert his constituency. Carleton was regarded as a safe seat for a Conservative leader, but did Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his supporters arrange to have a candidate oppose him? Not a bit of it; Sir Robert was allowed to be returned by acclamation. This is what any one at all fair-minded would have expected would be done. Later on Sir Robert Borden returned to the constituency of Halifax and was reelected there.
I need not go further with regard to my own record in this matter of elections, save to mention that in 1930. I was again returned to this house as member for Prince Albert by the handsome majority of 1,192. I would not have said what I have except for the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) has seen fit to insinuate that no constituency was prepared to retain me for very long as its member. Before touching

upon what the minister had to say with regard to the constituency itself, may I just add that, especially where one is in the position of leader of his party, I believe those he represents are quite sensible enough to entertain the view that the place at which they need representation is in the House of Commons at Ottawa and not necessarily in the constituency itself. It is a very fine tradition in the old country that a man may be free to reside in one part of the country and represent a constituency in another. I hope that that tradition will never fade from our parliamentary life because it offers the only means whereby many men who ought to be in public life can be brought into public life. If the tradition ceased to exist anything of the kind might no longer be possible.
It is true I have been unable to spend much time in the constituency I have the honour to represent in this parliament. This unfortunately has been equally true of the other constituencies I have represented. Although I have not been privileged to spend the time I would have liked to spend in Prince Albert, I do not think I have been neglectful in any particular of the interests of that constituency. I think hon. gentlemen opposite will find out that the good people of Prince Albert understand the situation pretty well, and will not be found lacking in appreciation of what I have endeavoured to do on their behalf.
Here is what the Minister of Agriculture said on Tuesday last with regard to the Prince Albert constituency. I will quote the passage in full, because I think it ought to be carefully preserved:
The right hon. leader of the opposition made one statement referring to the will of the people to which I take exception, and if the committee will bear with me for a few minutes i think I can show that he is not correct in his statement. The last redistribution made it impossible for the people in the federal constituency of Prince Albert to express their will. I have before me the results of the last federal elections and they show that poll after poll in the northern part, and especially in the city of Prince Albert and the districts in the neighbourhood of Prince Albert, returned majority after majority against the right hon. gentleman. This is what happened m the Anglo-Saxon and French speaking part of the constituency and the only thing that enabled him to carry the election were the votes of a large block of people of German descent who had been left in the southern Part of the seat in the last redistribution. I am not making any inference that these people should not be given every opportunity to exercise their franchise. They are of German descent. I had the privilege and pleasure of working throughout that whole district for years as a school inspector. Under the redis-

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
tribution which was in force during the last elections a large block of these people in the southern end of the Prince Albert constituency and another similar block to the north of Saskatoon, totalling in all about forty-five thousand progressive Mennonite farmers by being thus divided were practically denied the opportunity of nominating one of their own people so that this very worthy part of the Canadian population would be unable to express its opinion in this house. I know many of these people personally and they take second place to none, but this is what happened because of the work of scientific and highly specialized political racketeers. I do not think it was the work of the leaders of the Liberal party as we like to think of Liberalism. I believe it would have been a distinct gain if we could have as a member one of these people of German extraction who had made such a success. But that was made impossible because of the block left in Prince Albert constituency, evidently just to affect a vote of the people in the northern part of the constituency. By doing that, both these peoples have been practically disfranchised. The right hon. the leader of the opposition and his followers have therefore made it impossible for these people to express their will.
First of all let me say a word about people being disfranchised. What the Minister of Agriculture evidently had in mind was the Wartime Elections Act under which all the Mennonites were disfranchised, and under which, in some of ithe western communities, nearly everyone who happened to be of foreign origin was disfranchised. He just unconsciously let slip what was in the subconscious area of his mind-the thought of disfranchisement of Mennonites and others. There was no disfranchisement in 1930; everyone had a vote; everyone was entitled to vote as he thought best. What the minister could have meant by speaking of disfranchisement, unless unconsciously this thought crept into his mind, I am unable to understand, but what is interesting in connection with the minister's statement is this. He says that they were disfranchised, as he calls it, because the boundaries of the constituency had been so arranged as to bring these Mennonites and others into contact with the Anglo-Saxon people of Prince Albert; that the part of Prince Albert which votes Conservative was placed alongside this part of the constituency which votes Liberal. He says that this was "the work of scientific and highly specialized political racketeers." That, I shall show, was pretty hard on his own party, and on its past and present leaders.
I have taken pains to look at the redistribution of 1924 as it affected Prince Albert constituency. The Minister of Agriculture has sought to have it appear that this bringing together of these two elements and what
he calls disfranchising them, in that way, was the work of political racketeers, and he has tried to apply to the liberal party in 1924 that offensive designation. May I tell him that the constituency line of Prince Albert which determined that all these people shall be in the one riding, the Mennonites and the Anglo-Saxons, was the line laid down by Sir Robert Borden in the redistribution of 1914, a line moreover to which the present Prime Minister agreed, and for which he is part responsible. The southern boundary of the constituency of Prince Albert was left by the Liberal party in 1924 exactly where _ Sir Robert Borden and the present Prime Minister placed it in 1914.

Is it not a fact that the statement which my hon. friend has just made applies only to the eastern part of the present constituency of Prince Albert and does not apply to that part west of the third principal meridian?
I am speaking of the part referred to by the Minister of Agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture referred to the whole constituency.

I am speaking of the constituency of Prince Albert as it is now, and I say that the southern line was fixed by the government of Sir Robert Borden. It was agreed to by Liberals and Conservatives alike and the present Prime Minister was himself on the committee that determined it. I say that it was a right and proper line in 1914; I say that it was a right and proper line in 1924 and I say that it is the right and proper line for 1933.
I want to take direct issue with the view that the aim of a redistribution should be to segregate the different elements of our population. I believe in all our efforts with respect to the public life of our country and the making of a country, a nation, we ought to regard the citizens of Canada as Canadians, and Canadians only, irrespective of what their origin may be. The more we can get the different groups and classes which compose the nation to intermingle and understand each other, the more united and happy our country as a whole will be. I take direct issue with the Minister of Agriculture when he says that simply because some people happen to be bom of a different origin from his own, that an effort should be made in redistributing constituencies to have them placed in another district, so that they will in no way come into contact with those who happen to be English



Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
speaking; I do not think such a view is manly or British, or has anything to be said in support of it.
Let me say, with regard to the Mennonites
to whom the minister refers in the way he has, that there is no finer community of people to be found anywhere. As to their having the right to choose whomever they may wish as their representative, may I say that when in 1908 I was first nominated as a candidate for parliament, in the constituency of North Waterloo, the man who nominated me was Mr. Leander Bowman and the man who seconded my nomination paper was Mr. Henry Hostetler, each of whom belong to that community which my hon. friend said should be entitled to name a representative of their own for parliament. These gentlemen were outstanding citizens of North Waterloo, the constituency represented in this parliament at the present time by my hon. friend the exMinister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler). Is there any finer class of citizens to be found anywhere in Canada than is to be found in North Waterloo? Many of the Mennonites in the part I am speaking of in Prince Albert constituency come from the county of Waterloo itself. May I add this further fact, that when I was opposed in the by-election in Prince Albert in 1926, whoever was responsible for the choice of the Conservative candidate in that constituency chose Mr. J. G. Diefen-baker, to oppose me. It would seem he was of foreign origin. This gentleman, or at all events, his father whom I knew years ago, strangely enough came from the same county of Waterloo as I do myself. It ill becomes any minister of the crown to seek at this or any time to stir up racial strife and differences in this country.
The right hon. gentleman has done a great deal of it in his life.
It is all right for the Tories opposite to do it, but the minute a member of the opposition takes exception to their action, it is wrong so to do.
That is pretty small for the leader of the Liberal party.
I just draw attention to the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for interruptions and if they make interruptions, they must expect to get the replies they deserve.
May I appeal to hon. members in committee to allow tnis debate to be carried on without such frequent interruptions?

I thank you, Mr. Chairman.

May I now say a word in reference to the new boundaries of Prince Albert as set forth in the schedules that are before us. The government have brought down a redistribution map and they have presented to us the boundaries of Prince Albert among those of other constituencies. Let me first of all draw attention to the fact, .as I did the other day, that the average unit of representation for constituencies has been fixed at 44,186. Let me draw attention to this further fact. It has been admitted on all sides, that where there are cities there should be a larger unit of representation than in the rural districts. Now the constituency of Prince Albert has in it the fourth largest city in the province of Saskatchewan, the city of Prince Albert, which has about ten thousand population. The present constituency of Prince Albert has a population of 50,898. The map which hon. gentlemen have presented and which they ask us to accept reduces the total number of electors in the constituency of Prince Albert to 38,469. Though the unit in a rural district is 44,186, Prince Albert is reduced to 38,469 under the measure which is now before the house.
We are told that the problem which the committee was confronted with was to reduce the size of the constituency. How have they gone about reducing the size of the constituency? What they have done is first of all to add to the constituency on its eastern side a considerable part of the constituency of Melfort, the present seat of the Minister of Agriculture. I ask this house and the country, is there evidence of fair play with respect to a constituency that is to be reduced in size, when it is found necessary to begin by adding to it a considerable portion of another constituency? I have looked at the part that has been added to see if I could discover the reason why an addition should be made, and I think I have found it clearly enough in the fact that in the last general election the part which is added gave a considerable Conservative majority. It has been found desirable in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite to add to this already very large constituency of Prince Albert a part of a Conservative majority from another constituency.
What else have they done? They have taken away from Prince Albert a great part of the southern portion of the constituency. When one examines the constituency as a whole one finds exactly what was in the mind of the Minister of Agriculture when he said the other day that Prince Albert in all its

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
northern part had voted against me. He stated that on the floor of the house. He has had to do with the drafting of this map. He knows all about it. The part that voted against me he is allowing to remain in, but the part that supported me most- strongly in the last election is being taken out. The pre-eminently Liberal portion of the constituency is being taken away, and they have taken away so much that it has been found necessary to add something from another constituency so as to have a constituency which will look reasonably large. But even then the constituency which they have given me at the present time is considerably below the unit. They have reduced the constituency of Prince Albert, notwithstanding the fact that there is a city in it, to 38,469, when the unit of population even in the rural districts is placed at 44,000 odd. They have by this process of gerrymandering changed the Liberal majority of 1,192 which I received in 1930 into a Conservative majority of 967.
May I add this? Take a look at the other constituencies in Saskatchewan. Have any of them been reduced in this fashion? Last Mountain, a purely rural constituency, has according to this map a population of 48,657; Mackenzie, 47,458; Regina, 53,209; Saskatoon, 47,362; South Battleford, 47,084; Yorkton, 49,423. Does that look like a desire to be fair as between the different constituencies of Saskatchewan? The new constituency that has been created immediately to the south of Prince Albert has been given a population of 46,285, and it is made up largely or partly out of what has been taken away from Prince Albert. Prince Albert has been reduced to 38,469, eight thousand less than the population of the new constituency that has been created, and which is a purely rural constituency while Prince Albert has a very large and growing city in the very centre of the constituency. If that is not gerrymandering, Mr. Chairman, I do not know what is.
The Prime Minister has said:	If there is
any fault to find, if there is any injustice, we are here to remedy it. Now I have presented a case to him and I am going to leave it with him and the government. They must do whatever they think best.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say here and now that
the letter written by Mr. Turnbull and Mr. Totzke fixing the boundaries of the constituency will be accepted by the government.

The letter
written by Mr. Turnbull to Mr. Totzke was in reply to a plan that related to the province of Saskatchewan as a whole. It was 53719-343J
not a communication that had reference to the constituency of Prince Albert.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I mean the letter about
Prince Albert.

Pardon me, it was a letter that dealt with the general plan of the constituencies. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke) is here to speak for himself. He will say that he never proposed or agreed to anything that had not relation to the province as a whole, and the reason the committee did not come to an agreement was that they could not agree on the constituency of Prince Albert among other constituencies.
As the Prime Minister has requested it, Mr. Chairman, I am going to state to my hon. friend opposite what I believe in the circumstances to be a perfectly fair redistribution with respect to the constituency of Prince Albert, and I shall leave myself in the judgment of the house and the country as to whether what I suggest is or is not fair.
I have in my hand the constituency map of Prince Albert as it stands at the present time.
I notice that most of the constituencies in Saskatchewan -have their boundaries marked out by lines parallel both east and west and north and south.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The townships.

Yes, the townships are all framed on the square. What has happened in regard to these northern constituencies in previous redistributions and in the present redistribution has been to narrow the territory between the boundaries east and west. That is to say, the constituency is made narrower, and narrower for this reason, that the population continues to run up to the north. What is happening in the redistribution map in Saskatchewan is much like what one sees on the banks of the St. Lawrence in Quebec, where as the population has increased one will find a large farm which has come to be subdivided among the members of a family, in a manner which will give to all a certain frontage along the river. These northern constituencies run to an indefinite part of the country, a part not inhabited at all, and as the population continues to increase towards the north they have been made narrower. I say that that same process should be followed with respect to Prince Albert at the present time. It is being followed with regard to constituencies lying to either side of it.
The boundary on the east side is along range 24 west of the second meridian. The lower

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
part of the constituency of Prince Albert as it exists at the present time is on a range line between ranges 25 and 26. My suggestion to hon. gentlemen opposite, and it is only a suggestion of what I think is fair, is that the line which starts between ranges 25 and 26 at the southern part of the boundary be carried direct north, and that that portion of the constituency which lies to the east of that line be made a part of the adjoining constituency, I should be sorry to lose any part of the present constituency, but if the constituency is to be reduced in size this would appear to be the fairest way to all concerned to go about it.
I did not know when I looked at the map What would be the result of that arrangement politically. I may give to the house what I think is ;a correct statement, and that is that the total number that would be affected is something around four thousand. I think about four thousand, would be taken out of the constituency as it exists at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What would the population remain?

The population would remain about 46,000 as I gather it. At the present time it is 50,800, and if 4,000 were taken out 46,000 odd would be left. In my view 46,000 for Prince Albert constituency is a small enough unit. It is smaller than that of the constituency of Mackenzie, smaller than Last Mountain, smaller than Regina, smaller than Saskatoon. It would be the same as the new constituency of Hague. As a matter of fact, owing to the fact that there is a city in it, it should be one of the larger constituencies of the province. I have since looked to see, so far as I could figure from the results at the polls, what the effect would be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What is the population
of Prince Albert now?
Nearly 10,000.
It is 9,905.

Yes, about
10,000. As I figure it out as a result of the transfer I have suggested there would be a loss of Liberal votes. In round figures there would be a net Liberal loss of about 100 votes. It would take off, as I have figured it out-and I am subject to correction although I believe my figures are correct

it would take 4,420 from the present constituency which would mean a loss according to the 
figures of the last election of 678 Conservative votes and 761 Liberal votes, or in other words a net Liberal loss of 83. I know the government have to consider other constituencies, and that the addition of 83 Liberal votes to the Melfort division might occasion some concern. But I submit that that could be offset by a rearrangement of the line, elsewhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Leaving out the question of votes-because those of us in the west know that only small importance attaches to that from one time to another-what is the effect upon the population of the nearby ridings? I am asking that question for information.

The effect on
the population?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, by the addition.

Melfort, as
I see it here, is 36,237. It is a very small unit under the proposed map.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is
referring to Melfort?

Yes, it is an
adjoining riding. If 4,000 were added to it it would bring Melfort nearly to 40,000, leaving Prince Albert considerably lower than it is at present.

It is impossible to transfer those two ranges without retransferring to Melfort that portion on the east side of Prince Albert which has come from Melfort to Prince Albert, and about which the right hon. gentleman now complains. So in addition to transferring 4,400 of the Prince Albert vote there would be a transfer back to Melfort of 4,835. That along with the 39,000, at which Melfort will stand under the proposed redistribution, would bring the population of Melfort up to 48,853, with no city in it. In that way that constituency would be made much larger than Prince Albert which has a city in it.

I thank my
hon. friend for adding that which I had left out of my calculation. I was speaking of the constituencies as they are at the present time, and not what they would be under the new arrangement. I have another suggestion to make along the same line. I have not discussed it with the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) but I do not see, if it is necessary further to reduce Prince Albert, while I should be sorry indeed to lose any of those who reside in the western townships, why a line might not be taken on the west side of the constituency, in a

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
somewhat similar way. The line there also stretches far to- the north. I do object, however, to cutting out of the southern portion of Prince Albert constituency, a part which is cjuite thickly populated and which should be retained.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I must say at once that
I am most anxious as far as possible to meet the views of the right hon. gentleman. As my questions have indicated, the difficulty is that we would be leaving a rural constituency of 48,000 people without a town in it. It would be hardly fair to impose upon a government the necessity of accommodating an opponent to that extent. If there is any way out of it I should like to hear it.

I agree with
the right hon. gentleman that I should not ask the government to do anything for me which would embarrass the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, that is not the
point.

I do say, however, that if my right hon. friend will confer with hon. members in charge of the maps he will find it might be possible to take from the constituency of Melfort some part of what is now being given to it, which part could be added to one or other of the adjoining constituencies in a manner which would do no injustice to anyone. I do not know anything about the political complexion of these areas, but I do think something of that kind could be done. At all events I am quite content to leave the matter, so far as Prince Albert is concerned, with the Prime Minister and his colleagues.
I have only one other word to say, and that is *with respect to North Battleford. I understand it is the intention to change the name of north Battleford constituency to that of Bedberry. The city of North Battleford, the one which gives its name to the constituency, will probably disappear from Redberry, and the city which is now called North Battleford will go into what will afterwards be known as the Battlefords. I do submit that there is something in retaining names having an historical significance. North Battleford and South Battleford are names which have figured in the history of our country and it would, I submit, be a pity to have them disappear from the maps. Redberry may have some associations-I know it has with one very distinguished gentleman-but the name at present means but little to the people of Canada as a whole. The name of North
Battleford does mean something. The constituencies of North Battleford and South Battleford are separated by the Saskatchewan river. Further than that the constituency of North Battleford serves commercially that part of the country lying to the north of the river which will be included in the new constituency of Redberry. The business and community interests of the latter are bound up with North Battleford.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that Battleford was at one time what might be termed the capital of the Northwest Territories.
The old town.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the old town of
Battleford. Along the line of what the right hon. gentleman has said concerning the undesirability of perpetuating differences, I might say the idea is to follow the provincial lead and call them one community, namely the Battlefords, rather than accentuate the differences which have grown up between north and south.
They are joined together, provincially.
We do not follow the provinces.

I think elsewhere in the province provincial boundaries are not closely followed. I do think there would be a distinct advantage in retaining the name which has been associated with that particular part of the province. That which will be the new constituency of Redberry is in considerable part the old constituency of North Battleford. I believe if the government could see its way clear to retain the old name of North Battleford, rather than calling it Redberry, and would bring the town of North Battleford into that constituency, making whatever other adjustments they may find necessary and may wish to make with respect to the boundaries, they would at this stage settle any difference there may remain between us as regards that constituency.
I wish to say further that in view of the remarks of my right hon. friend in the course of the last half hour, if the government is prepared to reconsider and to meet us in the few particulars I have mentioned there would be no desire on our part further to discuss the situation in Saskatchewan. I do not for one moment admit that we are or would be satisfied with -the redistribution in the province as a whole, because we are not. But we

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
cannot expect to be satisfied. We realize hon. gentlemen opposite are in power, that they must and will have the last word, and also that they must take the responsibility for their say. I think the members on the Liberal side both in committee and in the house have made the strongest plea they can and1 have fought to the limit of their endurance in seeking to protect what they believe to be the interests of their own and other constituencies and of the electorate in the different parts of the province, and I do not want to lend encouragement to any further discussion if we can get this Saskatchewan situation settled by an amicable arrangement. I have made suggestions which I believe will at this stage lead to a settlement in that province, and at this point I am prepared to leave the matter in the hands of the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman will observe that the difficulty lies in the general disposition of the population; in shifting the boundaries of one constituency all are affected. I do not see how we can change the Battlefords if we are to maintain the relative population in the adjoining constituencies. I desire to assure the right hon. gentleman at once that I shall wait for a transcription of his remarks and endeavour to adjust tl?e Prince Albert situation in some way.

Perhaps as a member of the committee I might suggest a way by which that difficulty may be overcome. There is a certain portion of the proposed constituency of Redberry lying south of the Saskatchewan river. The population in that particular area is contiguous to the old town of Battleford, and this district contains a population of something like 4,000, if not more. This could be added to the constituency now called Battleford, and the transfer of the city to the constituency now called Redberry would not make so much difference with regard to the population.

I am very glad indeed to have the opportunity of saying another word or two with regard to my own riding. The other day in referring to the townships of Markham and Vaughan the right hon. gentleman said:
They were added, and when the general election came I carried the old constituency of North York but was defeated by the additional majority in the added townships.
That statement is not correct; the right hon. gentleman knows that he did not carry old North York, and he must have known it when he made that statement. I was dealing

with what he made reference to himself, the addition of the two rural townships of Markham and Vaughan, and while I was a little mistaken in the figures my right hon. friend was very badly beaten. Let us see what he says to-day; I took down his words. He said, "I repeat what I said before with respect to North York," and then he said that the reason for his defeat was the additional votes from Toronto. That was the reason he gave to-day; that was how he excused himself for being defeated in North York.
I would ask you to bear with me for a moment, Mr. Chairman, while I give the figures with respect to the Toronto vote in 1925 and 1930. In 1925, when my right hon. friend-not too friendly-was the representative of that riding, it was perfectly legitimate under the act to poll any person who had been living in the riding for two months prior to the date of the issuing of the writ; there was nothing wrong about it. Any man who came up there had the same right to vote under the law as it was then constituted as any person had who lived in the riding permanently. In 1928 or 1929 that vote was entirely eliminated, and so far as I was concerned I was confined, as was my opponent, to the resident vote. Now let me point out where the Toronto vote came in. We had Sutton, which includes Jackson's Point, which of course is the largest summer resort we have in North York; we have North Gwillimbury, which also borders on the lake and runs to Jackson's Point, and on the other side we have Georgina township. Those are the only three municipalities in my riding that come within miles of lake Simcoe.
Now let us see how fair my right hon. friend was, or perhaps I should say how mistaken he was. When we had this Toronto vote, Sutton gave my right hon. friend 179 votes and myself 300 votes; North Gwillimbury, which takes in Orchard Beach and other places, gave the right hon. gentleman 454 and myself 475, and Georgina gave my right hon. friend 411 and myself 367. So these three municipalities bordering on the lake gave the right hon. gentleman 1.044 votes and myself 1,146; my majority, which he says to-day resulted from the presence of the Toronto vote, was 102. Let us see what happened after the Toronto vote was cut off. because not a single soul from Toronto had the right to vote or did vote in 1930. In that year these three municipalities gave me a majority of 232 votes though not a single person from Toronto was permitted to vote. My right hon. friend stated that he was told by some person- that he had

Redistribution-Mr. Lennox
voted in both places. All I can say is that it must have been a friend of his who did so, because no one else would tell him. So we have the admission on the part of the right hon. gentleman that apparently his own friends voted in both places, because I am sure no friends of mine would vote twice and certainly if they did they would not tell him.
Now let me refer for a moment or two to what the right hon. gentleman said with regard to the sacrifices he made by going into constituencies that were not safe seats so far as he was concerned, and I dare say that would apply to a great many constituencies. I want to show his chivalry to the men and women who got out and worked night and day for him in North York. He ran first in the constituency of North Waterloo against Mr. Weichel, I believe, and was elected by a majority of 263 in the riding in which he was born. In 1917 he was defeated, in the same riding which knew him so well, by 315, and after his defeat he left the riding and never came back. In 1917 he was defeated by Liberals, because the leading Liberals were Unionists in the riding of North York.

That is not
correct.

Wait a moment; I would not get into trouble again if I were you. One of the outstanding Liberals who appeared upon the platform and worked tooth and nail against the right hon. gentleman was no less than the Liberal candidate in the provincial election in 1923, Mr. Pearson. And in Newmarket, which is preponderatingly Liberal, or was, there was a very large majority for Mr. Armstrong, if I remember rightly. That of course was in an election during the war. Then my right hon. friend went down to Prince Edward Island where he got an acclamation. Then he summons up courage and comes back to North York, and I may tell the committee that apart from the election during reciprocity, when Mr. Armstrong was elected by 59, prior to this, there never was, to my recollection a Tory elected in that riding. Sir William Mulock represented it for years, and by very large majorities; and Sir Allen Aylesworth represented it by very large majorities. So that the only time in my recollection when it was represented by a Tory, was at the reciprocity election of 1911, when practically the whole country went against my hon. friends, and during the war.
Then the right hon. gentleman was elected in 1921 by a majority of 1,055. He says that I was mistaken in my figures. Well, I was; I did not
know that I had beaten him so badly in the newly added portion of the territory. He was beaten by 408 in a riding that had never in its existence given a Conservative majority where there were two running. With 1,055 to his credit, a gerrymander took place-I should not say that; I should say a redistribution. In the election of 1921 he had 1,055, and he gave the house the impression that he was so very generouus in helping a Conservative candidate that he was willing to sacrifice himself, which he ultimately did in the election.
Let me say to the right hon. gentleman here to-day that in the election of 1921, taking in the new additions, the Liberal majority in Markham, Vaughan and the other municipalities that were added was 2,800; they got a majority of 2,800 over and above the number that voted for the Conservative candidate. And these are the municipalities which had snowed under the Conservative candidate in the immediately preceding election. My right hon. friend had the temerity the other day to get up and say that he added these places because he wanted to please the Conservative party.
I do not want to interrupt the hon. member, but I gave the house the figures, which are a matter of record.
The right hon. gentleman did not give them for 1921.

Yes; I stated
what the results of the 1921 election were in the total vote polled against the Liberal candidate.

At all events the right hon. gentleman was elected in 1921 by 1,055 in old North York, and in that same election, taking West York and South York, or East York as it was called, taking the two constituencies-because Vaughan is west and Markham is east of Yonge street-I may tell the right hon. gentleman, who never shirked anything, that there was a Liberal majority against the Conservative candidate in these sections that were added to North York of 2,800.

The hon. member is now talking about the combined majorities against the Conservative candidate. I gave the combined majorities against the Liberal candidate, and I think the house can determine which of us is right.

With respect to Vaughan and Markham, there is not a Conservative candidate who ever got a majority in the
Redistribution-Mr. Lennox

former township except Tom Wallace, who lived in Vaughan; and he obtained a Conservative majority against Mr. Dewart, who was a Liberal, a Toronto lawyer, and who ran at the time the market gardeners were supporting the Conservative party.
Now let me refer for a moment or two to something else. I might observe here that even during the Union election in 1917, when Mr. Wallace was a Conservative candidate and ran against a lawyer in Toronto, Mr. Denton, a nephew of the judge, Mr. Denton defeated the Union candidate by a majority of 40 or 50 in the township of Vaughan-4 have not the figures by me. But even at that time that township went Liberal.
My right hon. friend has rebuked the government and more especially the Prime Minister and the committee for their lack of chivalry towards him with respect to his position in Prince Albert. He says that Markham and these other places that were added were Conservative. Well, let me say this to him: We are taking Markham out and putting it into another riding so that he should not object to that. I say to this distinguished gentleman who is leader of the opposition: "Come on back to North York. You are boasting that we are going to be beaten in the next election. Well, I invite you to come back to North York. I have no intention of running again, but I will if you come. If you want to keep me in public life and you want to go out of it, you come back."
Let me say a word or two with respect to the chivalry or lack of chivalry on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and members of the committee. It is said that they should not have interfered with the right hon. gentleman's riding. What chivalry did the right hon. gentleman display when he deserted Waterloo, when he deserted North York after they had defeated him? What chivalry did he show to the men and women who had gone out day and night working to defeat me? I am told that he never even wrote a letter thanking the Liberals for their support.

I do not know who said to my hon. friend anything of the sort, but it is quite untrue. I am quite prepared to have my friends speak for themselves in that matter.
_ Mr. LENNOX: They spoke for themselves in 1926 and they never asked you to come back again. The fact is that upon every occasion, except one, the right hon. gentleman has never gone back to a riding in which he was defeated. Chivalry, courage, yes! My riding was preponderatingly Liberal. But what happened

after the redistribution? I had intended to retire from public life at the end of 1923; I intended to go back to my legal practice. What happened in 1924 when they all thought and I myself thought that I was not going to run again? After the redistribution of 1924 the Liberal papers taunted and goaded me and did everything they possibly could. They boasted that by reason of the redistribution they had a majority of 1,500. They were blowing around that I would not dare to enter the constituency to oppose my right hon. friend. I had no intention of opposing him but they drove me to it. I never went to the convention of over 1,200 people where I was nominated. They telephoned to me in Toronto and asked me to come up during the afternoon and I did so hours after my nomination had taken place. The night before at the Albany Club I met a deputation of 80 or 100 who asked me to run. I told them that I would not. The next day when I went to the convention and met the executive downstairs I still said that I would not run. I felt that I had done my duty, having had seven elections up to that time. I had three elections in two years and a half and two protests, both of which I won. What happened? Brave as I think I am, when I got up on the platform-
Hear, hear.
There is another brave man over there. '
What a man!

When I got upon the platform for the purpose of telling them I would not accept the nomination, in a moment of weakness I wilted and weakened and, finally accepted it. Believe me, when I accepted it I thought that the right hon. leader of the opposition was more popular than it afterwards turned out he was. He has drawn the attention of the committee to the fact that my majority was 76; he is wrong there, without the new addition, it was 89. That is just an error in addition but I made one myself the other day. I do not hold that against the right hon. gentleman. I ran down and got the figures after dinner as I did not expect to speak. I had not the slightest conception of the apparent unpopularity of the right hon. gentleman in Markham and Vaughan.
In the next election the right hon. gentleman had the opportunity to come back. He would not have been opposing any local man because they were looking around for a candidate. They brought in one of my warmest personal friends, Mr. Harry Sifton. He was brought in from Toronto and was a

Redistribution-Mr. Lennox
stranger to the people of North York, but he got a majority of 247 in Markham. He was totally unknown personally to the people. The liberal majority in the provincial house in 1926 was 1,184 in Markham alone and the liberal candidate was a farmer living in Scarborough while the premier lived in York, which adjoins Markham. In 1929 the Hon. Mr. Henry ran again and he was opposed by Mr. Saunders, a young lawyer who lived in Stouffville. Mr. Henry was a farmer and he was opposed by a lawyer in a constituency which was preponderatingly rural. There is only one village in Markham but the people gave this young lawyer who had only been practising a few years and who did not live in the riding a majority of 892 against the premier.
According to the figures of previous elections, I thought that the majority of the right hon. gentleman in the township of Markham would be 400 or 500, but much to my surprise this was reduced to 71. The right hon. gentleman said that he would have defeated the present member for North York if it had not been for the city vote. They had added no less than 13,000 people to my riding. I was an entire stranger to Markham which is south of my riding. I was an entire stranger in every municipality that had been added. Being somewhat of a practical politician I decided what I would do. I said to myself: You had better get down into Markham and Vaughan. I did not put in as many days in ole} North York as did my right hon. friend. He spoke in all the large centres; he had nine cabinet ministers speak for him in 1925 and all of them with the exception of one were defeated by coming into my riding. There was George Graham, Mr. Massey, Mr. Marler-the whole crowd of them. It served them right, they should not have come in; but they did. My right hon. friend stated that it was the new parts that had defeated him. That, of course, is incorrect, and I am sure my right hon. friend, if he were to try to explain the matter to-day, after what the Toronto Globe has said, would be only too glad to admit I am correct. But I had no idea that the townships of Vaughan and Markham, traditionally Grit, and the other municipalities such as Richmond Hill and Markham village which never gave a Conservative majority, would all, except Markham, which gave a majority of 87 against me, give me large majorities. So I begin to think perhaps that when the election of 1926 came along, my right hon. friend sought a constituency as far north from me as he possibly could get.
He speaks of Prince Albert and I am going to say just a word or two about that. My right hon. friend ran in a by-election in Prince Albert in 1926 and in that election he was opposed, not by a Conservative or anyone running as a Conservative, but by an Independent soldier candidate. In that election he got a majority of 5,621, and strange as it may appear the more the people of that constituency saw my right hon. friend and the better they knew -him, the smaller majority he got. When he ran in North York in 1921 he got a majority of 1,055 which was changed at a succeeding election into an adverse vote of 494, making a change in 1925 of between 1,500 and 1,600. In 1926, in Prince Albert, when he was opposed, I am told, by a Conservative candidate, he got a majority of 4,095. In 1930 he might have come back to North York, knowing there was at that time no Toronto vote which he said had defeated him in 1925, but having had a majority of over 5,000 in Prince Albert he remained as a candidate there and his majority was reduced by over 4.000. I do not see why there should be any difficulty about the Prince Albert riding. I would leave it as it is. If it reduced the Liberal majority from 5.600 to about 1,000, one can realize what the result would be in the next election, but I have nothing to do with the committee and for that reason I am not responsible foT what is being done.
I am not going to take up any more of the time of the committee except to say that the additions made no difference to my riding and to renew my cordial invitation to the right hon. gentleman, now that Markham is out Which he said was put in to help defeat him, to come back to North York at the next election and see how popular he is in that constituency.

Just a word in reply to a couple of remarks made by the hon. member for North York (Mr. Lennox). First of all, I noticed the other evening in discussing this bill he said that he wanted to have the riding of North York with the same boundaries as the provincial ones. I just want to say that the plan that was handed to the redistribution committee of the proposed future North York was handed to that committee before the provincial boundaries were fixed, so that the provincial boundaries are following the plan of redistribution that is shown by this map. I know something about my hon. friend's
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

courage and I do not think it is necessary for him to protest it as much as he did this afternoon. But what struck me as being rather remarkable is this: if he is as good a man as he was in 1924 and in the various contests bo which he referred-and I think, from his remarks, he is willing to admit he is- I am just wondering why he thought it should be necessary to get in the next election an advantage of about 1,100 more than he had during those previous campaigns.

So far as I am concerned, if I were running again, the boundaries would make no difference bo me; I would take a chance on any man who ran against me. I am not worrying about that, I do not propose to be a candidate at the next election and maybe the other candidate who will represent the Conservative party will not be as well known.
He may need the assistance.

Perhaps he may. What my hon. friend wanted was for me to consent to the old boundaries as they were; that is what he suggested to me, but I do not think he was serious in doing so. My hon. friend says that I am getting an advantage of 1,100. I am sure he will agree with me when I say that when I start within the boundaries of the old constituency I am from 800 to 1,000 in the red. Therefore if they gave me an advantage of 1,100, which they have not done, altogether the constituency would represent an advantage of only 200 or 300 Conservative votes. I have been fighting for ten years against an adverse majority of from 800 to LOCO and now perhaps some little concession should be given to me. I notice that the exMinister of Justice got all that was coming to him.
I am proud of the fact.

If we were all such wonderful men as the hon. member for North York, there need not be any difficulty about redistribution. So much has been said in this discussion with regard to my action and the action of the committee in connection with the redistribution of the constituency of Prince Albert that, while I have already expressed as well as I could what really has happened, still I think I must go over the matter once again. It has been charged that at one time I suggested a line running southeast and west to the south of the town of Duck Lake. I admit that that line was suggested, was talked of, but at the time that line was spoken of, I was trying to gat from the hon. member for 
Regina (Mr. Turnbull) an idea of just what he would do in connection with the constituency of Prince Albert. Prior to that I had been told that the southern boundary of Prince Albert would not be changed. I had been informed, not by the hon. member for Regina but by other hon. members from my province, that they were making the map and that there would be no alterations of any kind. Is it any wonder that there was not much opportunity for the hon. member for Regina and me to come to any agreement? But I want to say further that any suggestions which I made in connection with the constituency of Prince Albert were made as part of the general plan for the whole province. The hon. member for Regina said to-day that I had never agreed to the boundaries of any constituency as proposed by him. I say that that is true; I did not. There were a number of tentative agreements made between the hon. member for Regina and myself, but invariably these agreements struck a snag when we came to other portions of the province, and there was no agreement on any of them.
Also at the time I made the suggestion that the line might possibly go across at a point south of Duck Lake I also asked that the portion that had been taken into Prince Albert from the constituency of Melfort should be removed, but I was told that that could not possibly be done. I said to the hon. member for Regina, "I will look into this." After I had looked into it I went back to him and said, as I am sure he will admit, that that line would not do.
With regard to the proposal that I made at the time, that the territory that had been taken from the constituency of Melfort and put into the constituency of Prince Albert should be returned to Melfort, I want to read just one extract from the letter I received from the hon. member for Regina, dated March 25, very early in the negotiations. At page 3, section 7, he says:
I am also willing to consider the advisability of leaving the boundary line between Prince Albert and Melfort north of the north branch of the Saskatchewan river as it was.
The hon. member for Regina, and the Prime Minister in his remarks the other day, were very insistent that I had received an offer or a letter saying that the hon. member for Regina agreed with my suggested line.
I would like to read to the committee just what that offer was. It is in these words:
With regard to Prince Albert I will be prepared to make the southern boundary of that approximately on the line suggested by you.

Redistribution-Mr. Totzke
The only thing I want to reiterate in connection with this particular constituency is that the line suggested was part of a general plan. I was still working on a plan upon which I thought we might come to some agreement, and if that line had been proposed by itself certainly there would have been no agreement upon my part.
While I am on the constituency of Prince Albert I want to say just a few words in connection with some remarks that were made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) the other day. I do not intend to open up the controversy again. This is just a matter of figures that he presented and which I want to show to the committee could not possibly be correct. He made the statement that there was a solid German block or a block of Mennonites of German extraction of 45,000 people in the two constituencies of Prince Albert and Saskatoon. The population for the entire district of Prince Albert, according to the census returns, is 50,896, and according to the same returns the population for the city of Prince Albert itself is 9,905. The population as shown for Saskatoon constituency is 60,636, and the population for the city of Saskatoon is shown as 43,291, making the total for the two constituencies of Prince Albert and Saskatoon of 111,532 and for the two cities of Saskatoon and Prince Albert, 53,196. Subtracting the population of the cities from the total population of the two constituencies leaves a total of 58,336, and the Minister of Agriculture says that of this 58,336, 45,000 are German Mennonites or people of German extraction. That would leave a balance of 13,336 for all other races-Anglo-Saxon, French-speaking, Ukrainian and any other nationalities who may be living in that constituency. I say, Mr. Chairman, that that computation shows that the statement of the Minister of Agriculture is absolutely absurd. There cannot possibly be 45,000 of that particular class of population.
The Prime Minister the other day in his remarks on the province of Saskatchewan made much of the fact that the population was moving northward and that of necessity changes in the constituencies must be made in that province more nearly equalized to the population. We on this side have from the outset of the negotiations in connection with redistribution in our province taken the stand that all that was necessary, seeing that there was no change in the number of the representatives from our province, was to rearrange
the boundaries of the various constituencies in order that the population might be more nearly equalized. That was the idea behind any proposals and behind any map that we submitted.
The hon. member for Regina has made much of the fact that the redistribution of 1924 was a mistake, that in the central part of our province a certain number of constituencies were formed which should not have been formed and which were 18,000 below the unit of population. I want to deal for a few moments with that aspect of the question. The Prime Minister I am sure was quite sincere in his remarks, but I think I can show by the figures I am going to give that he did not have a clear picture of the situation in Saskatchewan.

I do not intend at this
time to discuss the northern portion of the province of Saskatchewan, but in connection with the southern portion of that province I should like to direct the attention of the committee to what I think are some glaring instances of unfair redistribution. This is the portion with regard to which the Prime Minister said recently we had come to an agreement. I want to say that never with regard to at least one of these constituencies have I agreed to the proposals of the government. I want to show the alterations that have been made in these constituencies, and I believe I can show that those alterations are unnecessary.
In the southeast corner of the province we have the constituency of Assiniboia. According to the last census, under the present

arrangement Assiniboia will have a population of 41,144. If hon. members will look at the map of Saskatchewan they will see that this is a very symmetrical, rectangular constituency; the north, south and west boundaries are almost straight lines. The east boundary has a few jogs in it, but those are correction lines in the townships. Hon. gentlemen opposite now -propose that this constituency shall -have a population of 40,946, and it seems to me that here they are not adhering to their policy of a proper redistribution of population. What have they done with that portion they are taking away? In the north comer they have taken off four townships and put them in the constituency of Qu'Appelle immediately to the north. Then they have taken a row of townships on the west side, a complete row extending the full length of the constituency, and put them into the constituency of Weyburn, although Weyburn did not particularly need it, because it has a population of 41,684. But what did they do to give it a little more population? In Assiniboia, instead of taking a straight line, they took four townships in the northeast comer and went up six miles, traversing three rows of townships, eighteen miles, and up another row of townships into Qu'Appelle, taking out these townships from the constituency of Qu'Appelle and putting them into Assiniboia. Let us see whether Qu'Appelle was too large in population and had to be reduced. Qu'Appelle, according to the last census, had a population of 35,938. It is a little small, and should be added to rather than taken from. But they took these places away and added more on the western end of Qu'Appelle in order to bring up the population a little, and we find as the final result of their manipulations here that Qu'Appelle has a population of 38,318. That is considerably below the unit, but perhaps the Prime Minister will say it has increased in population more rapidly than the constituency of Assiniboia. Let us see what happened.

Well, I have a grievance and it is my duty to state the position as I see it. I represent the Saskatchewan members in this matter and it is my duty to point out the mistakes that have been made. The Prime Minister has spoken about a perfect agreement in the constituency south of Qu'-Appelle. I say that we have not had a perfect agreement. There is one of the most glaring instances of unfair redistribution in the province. The population of Qu'Appelle
was low; it is not up to the unit. I want to give the percentage increase. I have already given it but I want to refresh the memory of hon. gentlemen. The percentage of increase in the constituency of Qu'Appelle was 8.8, which, compared with the increase in the northern constituency of Melfort, is very low. It is much below the average in the province of Saskatchewan. But that is not the particular complaint I have with respect to this constituency. I have always said that there was not so much complaint about discrepancies in population, but in this particular instance they have changed the straight line on the south side of Qu'Appelle and made a regular staircase of it. Starting with the eastern part, they go over a distance of twenty-four miles, then up six miles and over eighteen miles, then up six miles again, then over thirty miles, and then up to within about ten miles of Qu'Appelle valley. The only apparent reason for this alteration is, in my opinion, to try to secure a safe seat for the member representing Qu'Appelle and to ensure his return to this house. Now, I have no desire to see the hon. member for Qu'Appelle kept out of this house. I like him very much; he is a very nice chap and a good member. But in spite of what they have done for the hon. gentleman I am sure he will be left at home next time.
I say this is one instance where I could not come to an agreement with hon. gentlemen in regard to the southern part of Saskatchewan. The constituency of Weybum provides another example where the population was practically all right. But what have they done here? They have put another row of townships on the west side and taken off a few townships on the northwest comer. The constituency of Willow Bunch was too high in population and had to be out down, and I have no particular complaint to make in that regard. Maple Creek had a population of 43,903 and the percentage of growth was below the average of the province; still, they had to make some alterations. In Maple Creek, instead of adding a little to the population, they have made it 42,428. Moose Jaw is another instance where I could not agree. It had a population, according to the last census, of 42,334 and they have brought it to 43,668. They have added five townships and taken off a row of townships on the west side. Nine townships have been taken off from the west side. Moose Jaw constituency has the third largest city in the province of Saskatchewan, a city with a population of 21,000. Therefore, under the principle adopted generally by the redistribution committee, it has a little larger population
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

than some of the rural areas close to it. Moose Jaw now has a population, under the last proposal, of 43,668, and Willow Bunch has a population of 44,558. The next constituency, west of Moose Jaw, is Swift Current, which has a town of 5,000 people. Under this redistribution it is given a population of 46,447 as compared with Moose Jaw, 43,668.
Is it any wonder I said I could not agree to the redistribution in the southern part of Saskatchewan? There is'no question in my mind that these manipulations were carried out not with a view to equalizing population but with a view to making or trying to make safer the seats of hon. members occupying them behind the government. If that is the intention why do not hon. gentlemen say so? Why should they try to justify manipulations of this sort on any other ground? Moreover, there is in Qu'Appelle a glaring instance that has developed lately, and that is, taking a certain number of sections of land out of Qu'Appelle and throwing them into Melville 

just little sections, six I believe, with a population of perhaps 150 or 200. I believe the vote the last time was 11 to 77 or 79. It happened to be a Liberal vote because the Liberals had a pretty good majority. The excuse given for doing this is that it is more convenient for the people living in this poll to vote at Le Bret across the Qu'Appelle valley in the constituency of Melville. That may be so but I can give hundreds of instances where it would be more convenient for the people in one constituency to vote in a town in another constituency. If anyone will look at the map they will see how ridiculous it is. They start across the line of railways, then they go up across the line, come back again, up again and then back. There is no excuse for manipulation of that kind. It was bad enough before when its narrowest point was about ten miles wide. I know it will be said that that was done in 1924, but even so there is no particular justification for it. I am informed by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who was on>
the redistribution committee at that time, that he consulted with the then leader of the Conservative party from Saskatchewan, in another house, and this was one of the changes he asked for. This change was given to him. They have now made a jig-saw puzzle out of it. I wish I had cut it out because it is almost equal to some of those shown last evening. I think I have shown that there was no justification for the changes made in the constituencies south of the South Saskatchewan river and the Qu'Appelle valley.

Mr. Chairman, I do
not know whether I am in order but with great deference to yourself, I think I must say a few words. We like you in our province and we appreciate what you have done, but since you are interested in this matter and have taken an active part in discussing certain matters now before the committee, I think it would be only proper that you leave the chair and let some other hon. gentleman preside in your place.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose it is futile
for me to add any further protests to those already made by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke) in view of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said a few moments ago. He said: This is our plan and we are going to put it through. As has been suggested, I suppose that statement is based upon the fact that he has the majority.
I have represented the constituency of South Battleford in the province of Saskatchewan since the 1925 elections. For the information of the committee, I may say that this seat was created by the redistribution bill of 1924. It is proposed to eliminate this constituency by the redistribution bill now before us. If that is done, I suppose there will be one thing to my credit-I will have been the only member who has ever represented South Battleford in the federal house. Of course, that will be contingent upon the Prime Minister carrying out the threat he made a few moments ago.
I should like to direct attention to some of the glaring instances which have been referred to already during this debate. The constituency of South Battleford has a population of 45,119, and according to the figures given by the hon. member for Humboldt, there. are probably only eight or nine constituencies in the province of Saskatchewan with a smaller population. I suppose there is some reason for the elimination of South Battleford, but I would like to know what it is. I can conjecture as to why the present government is so keen to eliminate this seat. I join with the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) in protesting against the amalgamation of the two Battlefords. In my opinion it was wholly unnecessary to abandon any of the existing constituencies in Saskatchewan and create new ones. It has been argued all through this debate that the population in the north was growing faster than the population in the centre and south of the province. With that statement I am in entire

Redistribution-Mr. Vallance
agreement. It will be found that tihe constituencies in the extreme north of the province average some 50,000 in population. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Humboldt and by the Prime Minister himself, these constituencies have increased their populations to a greater extent than any others. In view of the argument adduced that the population in the north is growing at a faster rate and is likely to continue to grow at a faster rate, I think four constituencies could have been created instead of the present three. This could 'have been done without disturbing the province as a whole to any great extent.
I think if you were to take a group of individuals who were uninterested in redistribution and ask them what constituencies should be eliminated, they would answer: those with the smallest populations.
In spite of what the Prime Minister has said that this bill is going to go through, I rise to object to the joining of the two Battle-fords. They do not belong to each other. Those who know the geography of the province of Saskatchewan know that the northern Saskatchewan river has been the natural boundary between these two constituencies ever since they were created. In the southern part of the province the Qu'Appelle valley is recognized as a natural boundary. This valley can be crossed at practically every hundred yards but when you get away from the city of Battleford; the North Saskatchewan river can be crossed only by ferry. There are very few bridges and the two sides of the river do not lend themselves to amalgamation.
I am more opposed now than I was at the beginning of this discussion to the present system of redistribution in the various provinces. I am in absolute agreement with my leader. I think the province of Saskatchewan is an example of the abuses which can be resorted to under the present system. In spite of all that has been said, I contend that abuses have resulted.
Much as been said about the type of population in the different constituencies. If you look at the northern portion of the proposed constituency of Kindersley you will see that the five rows of townships which were previously at the south end of South Battleford are settled by Russians, Germans and other people from continental Europe. This type of population predominates over those from the motherland and the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It will be noted that in the last election in this constituency there was an overwhelming majority in favour of the Liberal candidate. In fact, the Conservative candidate made the statement that if 53719-344

Right in this city immediately after the last election during the special session of parliament, a western member, when he congratulated me on winning the election, said: "You have won this one, but you will not win the next; we will get you in the redistribution." I have listened with considerable interest to the debate on the redistribution bill and as yet have taken no part in it, *but I feel it is my duty to express my opinion regarding one or two matters. I have no grievance so far as my particular constituency is concerned, but before I sit down I want to make a suggestion with regard to the redistribution in Saskatchewan generally. Anyone looking at the map of that province will immediately realize how difficult it is to make an equal redistribution with regard to population. We have in that province twenty-one members, the same as we had formerly, but in studying the map one cannot help being struck by the fact that there are some natural boundaries which cannot or should not be overlooked in redistribution. We have such natural boundaries as the Saskatchewan river, which is navigable only at certain points by ferries and which should so far as possible be considered a natural boundary. Then we have the Qu'Appelle valley, which has always been and should be considered another natural boundary. In addition to that 
we have Long Lake, which divides the present constituency of Long Lake from that of Last Mountain, a lake about sixty or seventy miles in length and some three or four miles in width; that should be a natural boundary. In the redistribution map now before us I notice that the proposed constituency of Long Lake goes right around the borders on both sides of the lake. That seems to be a ridiculous proposition. That was the former situation, but it was changed ten years ago and in all fairness I think the proposed redistribution should be changed back again, so that the eastern boundary of Long Lake constituency will border on the lake called Long Lake.
I believe a sincere effort has been made to reach a satisfactory conclusion with regard to the redistribution in Saskatchewan. As I said before, I have no personal complaint because the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and I some time ago agreed with regard to the boundaries between our two constituencies, his riding lying immediately to the north of Assiniboia which I represent. In addition to that, the hon. member for Humboldt prepared a map, which was also agreeable to me, and his map added some population to my constituency to the west instead of to the north. Personally, it makes very little difference to me whether an addition is made one way or the other; I am satisfied with everything that will be a fair and equitable distribution of the whole province. I feel rather keenly the position in which some of my colleagues in Saskatchewan are placed in the redistribution which is now under discussion. I do not see that there is any necessity for eliminating one seat. That has meant now that the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) and the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) are in the one seat; one or other of them will be eliminated. Then we have the situation in Battleford which has been explained by the two members for that double constituency. Had it not been for the fact that some of my friends have been rather discriminated against in this redistribution, I should not have taken any part in this discussion. When it comes to malcing additions to any of the constituencies or changing the boundaries it must be remembered that in the western provinces the constituencies, especially in the rural districts, comprise very large areas, and we do not like the idea of having new territory added because we find it difficult now to keep in touch with our people and get acquainted with them even in several years when there is such a large territory to cover. For that reason we are averse to having additional territory added.
