Mr. Chairman, I shall not occupy many minutes of the committee's time. I wish, however, to say a few -words in regard to the situation as it concerns t'he Battle-ford constituencies. Hon. members of the committee will recall that the old town of Battleford was built many years ago on the south bank of the Saskatchewan river. That was before the days of railway building. The country around the town developed and was tributory to it. The town was the commercial centre. There was no settlement north of the river un-til the coming of the railway. When the Canadian Northern railway went through it opened up the north country, and as a result the town of North Battleford was established on the north bank of the river. That town became the commercial centre of the new territory opened up north of the river. At the last redistribution two constituencies were set up, South Battleford on the south bank of the river and North Battleford on the north bank, the river forming the natural boundary. That condition has been satisfactory. The proposal now is to take from North Battleford constituency a certain number of townships and add them to the South Battleford constituency. I cannot think that that was done with the object of gerrymandering a seat, because I have counted the votes at the last election, and I find that the Conservative majority in the piece of territory being taken from North Battleford and being put into South Battleford was only 153. I do not believe that 153 votes are going to determine how that seat will go in the next election. I venture to assert that whoever is elected in the the new Battlefords seat which is to be made, whether he be Conservative, Liberal, or C.C.F., will have a majority of more than 153 votes. He will have several times that many. I say therefore that the Conservative majority of 153 votes cannot be the determining factor. Why, then, do the government want to take territory from the North Battleford seat and place it in the seat across the river? The answer is obvious. Roughly speaking the population of North Battleford is 53,000, while the unit of population for the province is only 44,000. That is to say the population in the North Battleford seat as at present constituted is
9,000	too large. The proposal is to take some territory from that seat, and for equalization purposes to put in the seat across the river. In that piece of territory is the city of North Battleford. However the important consideration is this; Will the people in that territory be better represented in this parliament by one member sitting for all the territory north of the river, and representing 53,000 people, or by a member representing 43,000 north of the river and another member on the south side of the river representing	10,000 people north of the river
and several times as many south of it? I think that is the important consideration, and I do not believe there is much doubt in the mind of any fair minded person as to which course those people would prefer, or as to which scheme would give them the best representation. If you take that territory from North Battleford, with its commercial centre, the city of North Battleford; if you lift it out of that constituency and put it into another you are dividing the interests of North Battleford and taking away a piece of territory in which they have a common interest. You are adding that territory to a constituency which in the past, rightly or wrongly, has conceived itself to have interests not identical with those of the North Battleford seat. If you add that territory to South Battleford here is the condition that will arise:	The people north of the
river will say, "Let us run a man from the north of the river; let us get our own man in." The people south of the river will say, "Those fellows north of the river are trying to elect a local man. Let us see that they do not do so. We will run a man from the south of the river." Since the portion of the constituency south of the river is several times larger than the other portion, the southern portion will prevail, and the people of that portion which is taken from North Battleford, the portion lying north of the river, will always feel that they are not properly represented, and that their representative has a greater interest in furthering the cause of the portion of the district
Redistribution-Mr. Butcher

south of the river than in furthering the cause of the portion to the north. They will always feel that they have a grievance, and they will not be satisfied to remain in that situation; they will always want to get back to their old seat.
I believe that should be the paramount consideration in this matter. I think that is more important than considering whether 153 votes should go to one side or the other, and I think it is even more important than considering whether the population in each constituency is exactly the same. It is important that the population of each constituency should be as nearly equal as possible, but it is more important that those who have a community of interest should be placed in one seat, with those who have another community of interest placed in a different constituency. That is more important than the mere counting of heads. I submit that consideration to my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Turnbull) and the government generally, because I believe that if they consider the matter in that light they will admit that there is some justification in the claim of the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh) that this territory should be restored to him.

It will take me but a very few minutes to explain the situation in the constituency I have the honour to represent, Mr. Chairman. I cannot complain that several townships, with a majority of Conservatives, have been added to my constituency with the view of lessening the chances of the Liberal candidate in the future. I cannot complain that several townships preponderantly Liberal have been removed therefrom. I cannot complain that a large number of Liberals have been added to the constituency in order to limit the prospects of the Liberal candidate in an adjacent riding. I can only complain that sentence of death has been passed upon the constituency which I have the honour to represent. The execution is to take place at the next general election. The body is to be divided into three parts. One part is to be buried in the constituency of Melville, another in Yorkton and the third in Long Lake.
You have been advised already, Mr. Chairman, that the representation in the province of Saskatchewan will be the same after the next election as it has 'been during the last two parliaments. In the past we have had twenty-one members, and after "this bill is adopted we will still be entitled to twenty-one members. We agree with hon. gentleman

opposite that some sort of adjustment is necessary, because the population is not equalized as between the various constituencies. We were under the impression, however, that these adjustments might be accomplished by making alterations in boundaries, rather than by the elimination of some constituencies and the creation of others. Some of us supposed that because we were to have the same number of members it would not be necessary to make any change at all in the map, that we might continue with the constituencies we had in the past. We were informed, however, that there were objections to that course of procedure. One objection was that,some of the constituencies were too low in population while others were too high.
I found myself very much in accord with some of the principles enunciated by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) during the course of his remarks a few days ago. He said that a redistribution should be based upon the population as disclosed by the census; that the unit in urban constituencies should be greater than in rural constituencies, and that no greater disturbance should be made with regard to existing constituencies than was absolutely necessary. Bearing in mind these principles I took the trouble to analyze the results of the last redistribution as well as the results of the present measure. I find that after 1924 we had seven constituencies with populations of less than 41.000. while under the present measure we will have six. After 1924 we had seven constituencies with populations between 41,000 and 45.000; after this measure passes we will have eight. After 1924 we had seven constituencies with populations of more than 45,000; we are still to have seven. With regard to the central constituencies referred to by the hon. member for Regina, those of Long Lake, Melville, Last Mountain, Rosetown and Kindersley, there is no doubt that the population was very low indeed, but I am distinctly of the opinion that the map first presented by the hon. member for Humboldt rectified those irregularities. I found that the unit of population in Saskatchewan was 43.861 and that Regina was left with 56,186, Saskatoon with 52,823 and Kindersley with 39,775, while the eighteen other constituencies ranged between 40.601 and 44,494. It did seem to me that it was unnecessary to eliminate any constituency or create any new ones; for that reason I greatly deplore the passing of the constituency of Last Mountain, and I believe my feeling in that regard will be shared by my constituents.

We have all read that tragic story. I forget who was the captain of the vessel. It was not the captain of the Bright Fan. He got through better than the Bright Fan. It adds to the eastern side of the constituency of Prince Albert a section from the adjoining constituency, a section which brings into the constituency of Prince Albert an additional number of some four thousand persons, a part moreover which is largely Tory. Well, to reduce it by beginning to add to it does not seem bo me a fair way of proceeding. It is against that in the first place that I wish to protest.
Another objection I wish to make is this. The unit of representation of Prince Albert as it stands in the proposed redistribution is away below what is the unit of representation of rural constituencies generally in the province of Saskatchewan as they appear on the map. It is down to 38,469 in Prince Albert whereas the unit in a rural constituency is 44,186.
Not rural constituency but the average for all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the right hon. gentleman has confused two things.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING. The unit that is recognized, and my right hon. friend knows that where there are cities in a constituency we have pretty well agreed that the unit of representation should be above that in purely rural seats.
Certainly.

And I have pointed out that the city of Prince Albert is in the constituency of Prince Albert, and that the constituency as it appears on the electoral map should therefore have above the average unit of 44,186. It ought to have at least in addition another couple of thousand. That at all events is my view of what is fair and just .in the matter.
I would say further that the redistribution should seek to be impartial as between the political parties. If that may be considered a factor-I do not say it will necessarily be considered as such-but if it were to be considered as such the aim I think should be, where there has to be the taking away of any part of a constituency, that it should be taken away in a manner which will reduce in equal numbers or approximately equal numbers the representation of both political parties.
Those are the points that strike me as being fair. I am stating what I believe to be what the people of the constituency of Prince
5472	COMMONS
Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
Albert will regard as fair in the light of the position as it is. I do not wish hon. members on this side to keep up the discussion in order to attempt to force the hand of the government in any way as to what it is going to do in Prince Albert. I have stated the case so far as Prince Albert is concerned, and I propose to leave it at that and to abide, as of necessity I shall have to abide and the constituency will have to abide, by the decision of .the government in the matter. But I will expect the government to do. what they believe to be right, and they must be prepared to have their action judged in the light of the perfect freedom which they have in the matter of reaching a decision. I hope I am making clear the view I take. I am not asking for anything, personally. May I say to the hon. member for Regina that frequently this afternoon and in his remarks this evening he said my reason for stating my position was that I was afraid of something, that I was afraid of this or afraid of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was adopting the language of some hon. gentlemen opposite.

I have not heard any hon. member from this side saying any hon. gentlemen opposite were afraid.
Mr. BENNETT, Oh, yes.

I do not think so. At any rate, the hon. member is free to choose his own language. I just wish to say to him that I am not in the least afraid of the consequences of a campaign in Prince Albert, nor am I afraid of a general campaign whenever it may come, so far as the fortunes of the party which I have the honour to lead are concerned.
The same applies on this side of the house.

I have spoken longer than I had intended. We have come practically .to the closing hour of the day, but before taking my seat I should like to say just one word further about the Battleford constituencies. I do believe an injustice will be done if they are left in their present form. I mean, the form in which they appear in the redistribution map. Why should we seek the creation of new constituencies under new names, when at the present time we have names which form pant of the history of Canada associated with particular areas?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I draw the attention of the right hon. gentleman to one matter which concerns me, and with which
[Mr. Mackenzie Kincr.1
I have much difficulty. To change any one constituency in the area to which attention has been directed will necessitate the redrafting of the entire schedule concerning that area. It is a great difficulty. I know the right hon. gentleman opposite appreciates, as he did this afternoon, that the general quota is substantially the same in the whole area, obviously sometimes you have to add on in order that you may properly arrange the population-and this has nothing to do with politics. That was done in some of the seats to which reference has been made. The difficulty is if you change the Battleford constituencies and Prince Albert the whole matter is open again, and you have to rearrange all the northern part of the map. That was the stand taken by the representative on the committee: "You do this, and if you do not do it in the way in which we want it we will object to the whole." If the right hon. gentleman has any explanation I am most anxious to hear it-and I must say I have spent some time looking at the maps to-night. Just how it will be possible to follow his suggestion without recasting the whole, I cannot see.

May I say to
the Prime Minister that while it is perfectly true that in the negotiations, whatever proposals have been put forward from this side have been put forward in reference to a map which represented the constituencies as a whole, so far as the present stage of the discussion is concerned it is not our intention to attempt to continue the discussion on all constituencies. The hon. member for Regina has said some hon. members have not spoken, and he has concluded from that they were-
No, no. I said they had all spoken, but had not complained of their own ridings. .

It would be
a most extraordinary thing if a redistribution were made in which every member would be so badly treated that he would have to complain about his constituency.
It does not take much to bring complaints from that side of the house.

I am prepared to admit we are all inclined to search out and it is our duty to search out what appear to us to be insufficiencies or inaccuracies. I wish to say at the moment, however, that we do not intend to go over the entire map of Saskatchewan and hold up this House of Commons simply to have our own way with

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
respect to any map which has been presented.
I realize and have said from the start that the government has its majority. Further, the Prime Minister has made it clear that he intends to use that majority to have this redistribution put through. If it will facilitate conclusion of matters to have it known that our chief difference at the moment comes down to the constituency of Battleford, or Redberry as it is now proposed to call it, leaving the question of Prince Albert as I have left it, I would say that that, as matters stand, is the point of greatest importance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Does the right hon.
gentleman refer to the name or to the arrangement of the area?

What I have
in mind is that the constituency to be called Redberry should be permitted to retain the name of North Battleford. For the constituency to retain it appropriately the city of North Battleford, to which the whole commercial and industrial area in the north is related, ought, it seems to me, to be in it. And to arrange this is a matter of very slight readjustment, so far as I can see, because there is only the distance of six miles from the boundary of Redberry to North Battleford. Furthermore, the city of North Battleford is not very large. So far as we are concerned, I think we would approve of any adjustment by hon. members opposite which could be recognized as fair, even if it were to involve taking a corresponding population from one constituency and adding them to another.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Speaking from memory,
I must say to the right hon. gentleman that to do what he suggests will necessitate a change in the constituency directly south, namely that of Kindersley. That matter was considered by the committee, and they found it impossible to adjust the population basis if the boundary of the new projected constituency of North Battleford were carried farther south and took in part of Kindersley. That would make an adjustment necessary in that area, and so on throughout, and the whole map north of the Saskatchewan river would have to be recast. The right hon. gentleman must appreciate that that is the real difficulty. I have looked at the map with great care to-night and I really do not see, in view of the arrangements which have been arrived at with regard to the general principles of equality of population, how such a change could be made. I make that statement frankly.

We have
reached the hour for adjournment. I should like to ask the Prime Minister to take another look at the map to-night, to see if it is not possible, without in any way prejudicing the map as a Whole, to make the slight readjustments which ought to be made. I have looked at it and I must say I cannot agree when he states that to do this will in any way upset the whole arrangement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did the right hon. gentleman look at the Kindersley situation?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And Rosthern?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And Rosetown?

Yes. I think
it is quite possible to take part of the immediate environment as between the two Battlefords themselves and make the necessary adjustment. However I shall leave the matter in the hands of the right hon. gentleman.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put pursuant to standing order.
Friday, May 26, 1933
